name: Zanzibar
tagline: Swahili spice island of dhows, coral lanes and turquoise sea.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Sep, Oct, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: The long dry season from June to October is ideal, with February bringing Sauti za Busara and its own dry spell; skip the long rains of March to May.

ourTake.lede: Stone Town rewards a day or two of unhurried wandering, then the north and east coasts are where you settle, Nungwi and Matemwe for reliable swimming, the southeast for quiet. Skip the packaged spice tours and the overbuilt Kendwa strip; hire a private guide who actually knows the farms and the alleys. Tides here are dramatic, so pick your beach for whether you want to swim at all hours or don't mind walking out at low water.
ourTake.comeIf: You want white-sand indulgence paired with a spice-island soul, ideally bookended with a mainland safari.
ourTake.skipIf: You want a lively city break or reliably kosher-clean street food and nightlife on tap.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: &Beyond Mnemba Island
items.area: Mnemba (private island, off the north-east coast)
credentials: &Beyond, flagship Indian Ocean private-island lodge
Ringed by the Mnemba Island Marine Conservation Area (MIMCA)
items.description: The icon, a barefoot private island of twelve open-fronted bandas, and the address every other Zanzibar resort is measured against.

items.name: Zuri Zanzibar
credentials: Design Hotels member
Private tide-free beach at Kendwa, all-day swimming
items.description: A design-led garden village above a rare tide-free west-facing beach, the north-coast address with genuine architectural intent.

items.name: Xanadu Luxury Villas & Retreat
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) member
National Geographic Traveller (UK), Middle East & Africa Collection 2024
items.description: An intimate, adults-leaning villa hideaway that trades scale for privacy and polish.

items.name: The Residence Zanzibar
credentials: Cenizaro, The Residence collection
Spa rated among Africa's top 10 by Condé Nast Traveller (2024)
items.description: Sixty-six private villas, each with a plunge pool, spread through 32 hectares of garden on a mile-long beach, the grand family estate.

items.name: Park Hyatt Zanzibar
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller Readers' Choice Awards 2025, No. 3 Best Hotel in Africa
Set on the Stone Town seafront, a UNESCO World Heritage site
items.description: The one true luxury address inside the UNESCO old town, a restored seafront palace where history is at the door and the beach at your feet.

items.name: Baraza Resort & Spa
credentials: The Zanzibar Collection, award-winning luxury group
Frangipani Spa recommended by Condé Nast Johansens
items.description: Palatial Swahili-Persian-Omani architecture and all-inclusive ease, the most ornate house on the east coast.

items.name: Zanzibar White Sand Luxury Villas & Spa
credentials: Relais & Châteaux member
items.description: The island's Relais & Châteaux house, private villas, a serious spa and a beachfront on the kite-surfing coast.

items.name: Elewana Kilindi Zanzibar
credentials: Elewana Collection (Minor Hotels)
World Luxury Hotel Awards, Luxury Beach Villa, Africa (2018)
items.description: White-domed pavilions in 50 acres of garden, an eccentric, romantic hideaway originally conceived for an ABBA founder.

items.name: Matemwe Lodge
credentials: Asilia Africa, luxury eco-lodge collection
Faces the Mnemba Island Marine Conservation Area (MIMCA)
items.description: A relaxed, characterful lodge on the reef directly facing Mnemba, the closest mainland base to the island's best diving.

items.name: Zawadi Hotel
credentials: The Zanzibar Collection / Zawadi, boutique villa hotel
Cliff-top setting with private beach access on the quiet south-east coast
items.description: Nine cliff-top villas above an unspoiled beach, small, serene and thoroughly private.

items.name: The Stone Town heritage walk
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: A slow morning through the coral-stone labyrinth of the old town, where Omani-Arab, Persian, Indian and Swahili worlds fused over a thousand years of Indian Ocean trade. For an Indian family the connection is intimate and immediate: Gujarati and Cutchi merchant houses, Hindu temples and Ismaili buildings sit among the mosques and the carved doors. A private cultural guide reads the layers street by street in the cool before the heat.

items.name: The carved Zanzibari doors
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: Hundreds of monumental hand-carved doors are the signature of Stone Town, each a statement of the family behind it, Arab doors ornamented with Quranic script, elegantly plain Swahili doors, and Indian doors studded with heavy brass bosses that once warded off elephants back home in the subcontinent. Walking with a guide who decodes the lotus, the fish and the frankincense-chain motifs turns a photo-stop into a genuine reading of the city's mixed soul.

items.name: The House of Wonders (Beit-al-Ajaib)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: The grandest building on the seafront, the first in Zanzibar with electricity and a lift, built in 1883 for Sultan Barghash, its tiered verandahs and clock tower long the emblem of the town. Note: the facade and clock tower collapsed in 2020 and the building remains closed and under a slow UNESCO-supported restoration, so it is admired from Forodhani for now rather than entered. A guide gives the context that makes the shrouded shell legible.

items.name: The Old Fort (Ngome Kongwe)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: The oldest standing building in Stone Town, raised by the Omanis around 1698-1701 on the ruins of a Portuguese chapel after they drove the Portuguese out. Its thick coral ramparts now enclose craft stalls, a café and an open-air amphitheatre that hosts the Sauti za Busara music festival and the Zanzibar film festival. An easy, shaded first stop that anchors the whole seafront cluster.

items.name: The Sultan's Palace Museum (Beit el-Sahel)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: The former residence of the Sultans of Zanzibar, now a museum of the dynasty's daily life, the furniture, the portraits and the belongings of Princess Salme, the sultan's daughter who eloped to Germany and wrote the first memoir by an Arab woman. A short walk from the Old Fort, it gives the human, domestic side of the Omani court that ruled this Indian Ocean crossroads.

items.name: Forodhani Gardens night food market
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: Every evening the seafront gardens fill with grills and lanterns for East Africa's most famous street-food market, grilled seafood, Zanzibar pizza, urojo soup, sugar-cane juice pressed on the spot, all facing the water as the sun drops behind the dhows. Vegetarian and Jain guests do well here with the chapati, samosa, cassava and fresh-pressed juices, and a guide can steer the family to the cleanest, freshest stalls.

items.name: The Anglican Cathedral & the former Slave Market
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: Christ Church Cathedral was built from 1873 on the site of East Africa's largest slave market, its altar placed exactly where captives were once whipped, as a deliberate monument to abolition. The adjoining East Africa Slavery Museum and the surviving underground holding chambers make this the most moving and important hour in Stone Town, sober, well-told history that repays a private, unhurried guided visit.

items.name: The Freddie Mercury Museum
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: Freddie Mercury, born Farrokh Bulsara to a Parsi family from Gujarat, spent his early childhood in Zanzibar, and the museum near Kenyatta Road tells his story through photographs, memorabilia and the Zanzibari-Parsi world he came from. A quietly resonant stop for Indian visitors: the Indian-Ocean Parsi thread running straight from Bombay through Zanzibar to Queen. (His actual family home nearby remains a private residence.)

items.name: Darajani Market
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: The chaotic, sensory heart of everyday Zanzibar since 1904, pyramids of cloves, cinnamon bark, vanilla and chillies, fish and fruit and bolts of kanga cloth. For a subcontinental palate the spice hall is instantly familiar yet wilder, and a guided early-morning walk (before the heat and the crowds) is the best way to understand why this is called the Spice Island.

items.name: The Hamamni Persian Baths
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: The first public baths in Zanzibar, built between 1870 and 1888 for Sultan Barghash and designed by Shirazi-Persian architects, the hot rooms, cold rooms and cisterns still trace the old hammam ritual though the water is long gone. A small, atmospheric, easily-missed stop that rewards the curious traveller and adds the Persian layer to the Arab-Indian-African story.

items.name: The Old Dispensary (Ithnashiri Dispensary)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: The most exuberant building on the waterfront, a green-and-cream confection of carved wooden balconies and stained glass, built in the 1890s by Tharia Topan, a Gujarati Ismaili merchant and financier to the sultan, as a charitable dispensary. It is the single clearest monument to the Indian community that helped build and bank Zanzibar, and a natural, meaningful stop for Indian visitors.

items.name: The Dhow Countries Music Academy
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Stone Town of Zanzibar (inscribed 2000)
items.description: The living heart of Zanzibar's music, the academy that preserves taarab, the swirling Arab-Indian-Swahili orchestral song of the islands, along with ngoma and kidumbak. An intimate evening concert or a private taarab session here is one of the most authentic cultural experiences in Stone Town, and the Indian melodic lineage in the music is unmistakable to a subcontinental ear.

items.name: Dinner at the Emerson Spice rooftop tea house
items.description: A single nightly sitting on the highest rooftop in Stone Town, in a restored merchant's palace, where a set Swahili-fusion seafood menu is served as the muezzin's call rolls across the coral rooftops at sunset, sometimes with live taarab. Reservation-only and quietly theatrical, the most romantic table in the old town, and a natural honeymoon dinner. Ask ahead and they will build a vegetarian menu.

items.name: The Mtoni Palace ruins
items.description: The oldest and largest of the sultans' palaces, built for Seyyid Said around 1828 just north of town, roofless coral halls and arabesque arches now open to the sea and the wild, once home to the sultan's wives and hundreds of children, including Princess Salme. Sunset here, with a candle-lit history talk, is a quiet, atmospheric antidote to the busier sights.

items.name: The Maruhubi Palace ruins
items.description: The romantic ruins of the palace Sultan Barghash built in 1882 for his large household, its stone pillars and lily-pad reservoir standing in a quiet garden beside a working dhow-building beach. Overlooked by most day-trippers, it makes a peaceful, photogenic pairing with Mtoni for those who want the sultans' story away from the crowds.

items.name: Nungwi beach
items.description: The island's headline beach on the far northern tip, powder sand, turquoise water and, crucially, minimal tide so you can actually swim at any hour, unlike the east coast. It is the hub of Zanzibar's grandest resorts and the working dhow-building village, and the west-facing angle delivers celebrated sunsets. The natural base for a first-timer or a family that wants dependable swimming.

items.name: Kendwa beach
items.description: Nungwi's calmer, softer sister a few kilometres south, a broad west-facing strand famous for the most spectacular sunsets on the island and, again, water deep enough to swim at all tides. Quieter and more laid-back than Nungwi by day, it is the classic spot for a sundowner dhow and a barefoot dinner on the sand.

items.name: Matemwe beach
items.description: A long, quiet, authentic stretch of the northeast coast, still lined with fishing villages and seaweed plots, and the closest mainland beach to the Mnemba Atoll, the launch point for the island's best snorkelling and diving. It suits travellers who want serious marine life and genuine Swahili village texture rather than a resort strip, with a handful of superb boutique lodges strung along the shore.

items.name: Paje beach
items.description: The kitesurfing capital of the Indian Ocean, a wide, flat, reef-protected lagoon with steady trade winds that draws kiters from around the world, and a young, easy beach-shack scene. The east-coast tide pulls back nearly a kilometre twice a day, turning the shallows into a mirror-flat walkable flat; time your swims to the tide and enjoy the theatre of the water disappearing and returning.

items.name: Jambiani beach
items.description: The quietest, most traditional of the east-coast villages, a long ribbon of white sand where daily life still turns on fishing and seaweed farming, the women tending their green plots at low tide, wooden boats resting on the flats. For a couple wanting the real, unhurried Swahili coast rather than a resort, this is the most soulful choice on the island.

items.name: The seaweed farms of the east coast
items.description: At low tide the shallows off Paje and Jambiani reveal neat green plots tended almost entirely by women, Zanzibar's seaweed is a major export and, increasingly, the base for artisanal soaps and cosmetics. A gentle guided walk out onto the flats with a seaweed farmer is a rare, grounding encounter with the island's real economy and its women's livelihoods, well away from the beach-club scene.

items.name: Michamvi peninsula & Michamvi Kae
items.description: The narrow finger of land at the southern end of the east coast, the only place on the east coast where you can watch the sun set over the water, since the tip faces west across Chwaka Bay. Quiet, exclusive and home to some of the island's most private villas and beach clubs, it pairs an east-coast morning with a rare east-coast sunset. The Rock sits just off its shore.

items.name: The Rock Restaurant
items.description: The single most photographed table in Zanzibar, a tiny seafood restaurant perched on a coral outcrop off Michamvi Pingwe beach, reached on foot at low tide and by short boat at high tide, with the Indian Ocean on every side. The Swahili-Italian menu is secondary to the setting; book the sunset sitting well ahead, and ask for the vegetarian pasta and grilled-vegetable options.

items.name: Jozani Chwaka Bay National Park
items.description: Zanzibar's only national park and the last refuge of the endangered Zanzibar red colobus monkey, found nowhere else on Earth, troops of thirty-plus are all but guaranteed on the short forest trail, unbothered by visitors. The park pairs the primate walk with an elevated boardwalk over a mangrove forest, a gentle, shaded, family-friendly slice of the island's wild interior.

items.name: A spice-farm tour
items.description: This is why they call it the Spice Island, a walk through a working plantation where a guide cracks open cloves, nutmeg, cinnamon bark, cardamom, vanilla and lipstick-fruit, and you smell and taste each one straight from the tree. For an Indian visitor it is a vivid full circle: these are the spices the monsoon-trade dhows carried between Zanzibar and the subcontinent for centuries. Best done privately, with a Swahili lunch to follow.

items.name: Prison Island (Changuu) & the giant tortoises
items.description: A twenty-minute dhow ride from Stone Town to a small coral island whose sanctuary shelters a colony of Aldabra giant tortoises, a gift from the Seychelles in 1919, the oldest of them well over a century old, and gentle enough to hand-feed spinach. The old quarantine buildings and a house-reef for snorkelling round out an easy, delightful half-day, especially with children.

items.name: Snorkelling & diving at Mnemba Atoll
items.description: The finest reef in Zanzibar, a protected marine conservation area ringing the private Mnemba Island, its clear water alive with green turtles, dolphins, reef fish and, in season, larger pelagics. Snorkellers and divers launch from Matemwe or Nungwi; the atoll itself surrounds &Beyond Mnemba Island, so the surrounding water is kept pristine. The island's marine highlight, and a bucket-list snorkel for a honeymoon.

items.name: &Beyond Mnemba Island (the private island)
items.description: The most exclusive address in the Indian Ocean off East Africa, a single tiny private island of just twelve open-fronted casuarina-shaded bandas, ringed by its own reef, the definition of a barefoot-luxury honeymoon. It is the natural coastal finale to a bush-and-beach itinerary with &Beyond's Serengeti and Ngorongoro lodges, seamlessly linked by private air. Even for non-guests, the atoll around it is the island's best water.

items.name: The Nakupenda sandbank
items.description: A pure white ribbon of sand that rises from the sea at low tide off Stone Town, its name means 'I love you' in Swahili, where the classic outing is a private dhow, a snorkel over the reef, and a fresh-seafood lunch laid out on the bare sandbank with nothing around you but turquoise water. As castaway-romantic as the island gets, and easily arranged as a private charter.

items.name: The Safari Blue full-day dhow excursion
items.description: The island's classic full-day sail, a traditional dhow through the Menai Bay conservation area with snorkelling over coral, a swim in a mangrove lagoon, dolphin-spotting and a lavish seafood barbecue on a sandbank with tropical fruit and, for the brave, baobab-flavoured local spirit. Book it as a private charter rather than a group boat and it becomes an unhurried, genuinely luxurious day at sea.

items.name: The Maalum natural swimming pool
items.description: A hidden cenote-like pool in a collapsed limestone cavern near Paje, cool, clear, jade-green water in a jungle-fringed grotto, with a limited number of timed slots each day to keep it serene. It is the island's most stylish swim, quietly exclusive and Instagram-famous, and a refreshing counterpoint to the salt water of the coast. Book ahead; slots sell out.

items.name: The Kuza Cave
items.description: A turquoise freshwater pool inside a limestone cave near Jambiani, held sacred by the local Swahili community and open for a quiet swim in water hundreds of thousands of years in the making. It doubles as a small cultural centre teaching Swahili cooking, drumming and language, so a visit can pair a cool swim with a genuine, low-key cultural encounter.

items.name: Kizimkazi dolphins
items.description: The fishing village on the island's southern tip is the classic launch point for meeting the resident bottlenose and humpback dolphins of the Menai Bay conservation area. Go at dawn, with a responsible operator who keeps a respectful distance, and it becomes a magical rather than a chaotic encounter, best paired with the ancient mosque next door and a quiet southern lunch.

items.name: The Kizimkazi (Dimbani) Mosque
items.description: One of the oldest Islamic buildings in East Africa, its Kufic inscription dating the foundation to 1107 CE, a modest coral-stone mosque that marks the arrival of the Shirazi-Persian settlers who seeded Zanzibar's Islamic and Swahili culture. Understated and deeply historic, it gives real weight to a southern day out and is easily combined with the Kizimkazi dolphins.

items.name: Swimming with rescued turtles at Nungwi
items.description: At the Mnarani Marine Turtle Conservation Pond in Nungwi you can snorkel alongside green turtles in a natural tidal lagoon, the more conservation-focused of the village's two lagoons, which rescues turtles injured in fishing nets, rears hatchlings and runs release programmes. Framed as a conservation visit rather than a petting-zoo, it is a gentle, meaningful encounter, especially with children; ask your advisor to route you to the rehabilitation-led pond.

items.name: A sunset dhow cruise
items.description: The quintessential Zanzibar evening, a lateen-sailed wooden dhow slipping out from the west-facing north coast as the sky turns copper, a glass in hand and the crew easing the great triangular sail across the wind. On a private charter with sundowners and canapés it is the simplest, most romantic hour on the island, and the definitive honeymoon photograph.

items.name: Deep-sea fishing off the north coast
items.description: The deep blue water off Zanzibar's northern shelf is prime big-game territory, sailfish, marlin, tuna, wahoo and dorado run here, best from the north-coast marinas. A private sport-fishing charter (catch-and-release for billfish) makes a thrilling half-day for the keen angler in the family, with the crew handling everything and the catch cooked back at the lodge.

items.name: Cheetah's Rock
items.description: A small, fiercely ethical wildlife rescue where a strictly capped number of guests each day meet rehabilitated big cats, lemurs, otters and more in intimate, welfare-first encounters led by the founder, a rare chance to be close to African wildlife without the safari drive. Book far ahead; the tiny daily quota is the point, and it makes a memorable land-based half-day for families.

items.name: The bush-and-beach safari combination
items.description: Zanzibar's greatest role for the Indian traveller is as the beach half of Tanzania's classic 'bush and beach', the Serengeti's great migration and the Ngorongoro Crater's dense game, then a short flight to unwind on the Indian Ocean. The lodges connect by private air with no long transfers, making it the definitive East African honeymoon and multi-generational trip. Your advisor sequences safari, flight and villa as one seamless journey.

items.name: A stay at Zuri Zanzibar
items.description: One of the island's most design-forward resorts, a village of thatched villas cascading down to a swimmable Kendwa beach, with a serious wellness and spa focus and a globally-minded kitchen. Its sunset-facing north-coast position, calm water and polished service make it a strong choice for couples and families who want contemporary luxury over colonial nostalgia. A natural coastal base after safari.

items.name: A stay at The Residence Zanzibar
items.description: A serene 66-villa estate spread over palm-fringed grounds on the quiet south coast, every villa with its own pool and butler, the island's benchmark for a private-villa family holiday, with an unusually good, fully-supervised kids' club that frees parents for a spa day or a dhow. The gentle southern setting suits multi-generational groups who want space, privacy and calm over the busier north.

items.name: A stay at Xanadu Villas & Retreat
items.description: An adults-only collection of just nine private villas set in tropical gardens above a quiet east-coast beach, small, intensely personal and built around privacy, it is one of the island's most sought-after honeymoon addresses. The scale is the appeal: barely a handful of couples in residence at a time, with the attention and discretion an Indian UHNI honeymooner expects.

items.name: The Zanzibar Butterfly Centre
items.description: A community-run tropical butterfly house beside Jozani Forest, where hundreds of native Zanzibari butterflies fly free through a netted garden and a guide walks you through the whole life cycle. Small, shaded and gentle, it is a lovely, low-key add-on to a Jozani morning and a particular hit with children, while its earnings support the surrounding village.

items.name: A Stone Town cooking class & spice lunch
items.description: The most delicious way into Swahili culture, a market visit for the day's fish and spices, then a hands-on lesson in the island's Indian-Ocean cooking: coconut curries, pilau, chapati and the clove-and-cardamom notes that a subcontinental cook will recognise at once. Easily made fully vegetarian or Jain, and a warm, hands-on afternoon that connects the family straight to the Spice Island's kitchen.

items.name: The Rock Restaurant
credentials: Globally iconic standalone restaurant, a Zanzibar landmark
Free boat shuttle from the beach at high tide
items.description: A single dining room perched on a coral outcrop in the ocean, reached on foot at low tide or by boat at high, one of the most photographed tables on earth.

items.name: Emerson Spice Rooftop Tea House
credentials: Emerson Zanzibar, Stone Town's celebrated rooftop tea-house dining
Set atop a restored Stone Town heritage mansion
items.description: A seven-course seafood tasting served cross-legged on cushions atop a restored merchant's mansion, with a 360° view over minarets, spires and the sea as the call to prayer rolls across the rooftops.

items.name: Tea House Restaurant, Emerson on Hurumzi
credentials: Emerson Zanzibar, Emerson on Hurumzi rooftop tea house
Live Taarab performance most evenings
items.description: The highest rooftop in Stone Town, a set Zanzibari menu at sunset with live Taarab music from the Dhow Countries Music Academy.

items.name: Resort signature tables
credentials: In-resort signature dining at the credentialed maison houses (&Beyond Mnemba, The Residence, Baraza, Xanadu)
items.description: Zanzibar's most considered kitchens sit inside the maison resorts, private-beach dinners, dhow-deck lunches and spice-led Swahili menus arranged for house guests.

items.name: 6 Degrees South Grill & Wine Bar
credentials: Long-standing Shangani seafront grill and wine bar
Rooftop terraces over the Stone Town waterfront
items.description: Shangani's most reliably good table, Afro-Continental grill and a proper wine list across three sea-facing terraces.

items.name: Zanzibar Serena Hotel, Rooftop & Swahili Nights
credentials: Zanzibar Serena Hotel, restored 18th/19th-century seafront landmark
Weekly Swahili Nights with live Taarab music
items.description: A rooftop over the Indian Ocean and a Friday poolside Swahili Nights buffet with live Taarab, dining inside two restored heritage seafront buildings.

items.name: Forodhani Night Market
credentials: Forodhani Gardens, Stone Town's nightly waterfront food market
On the UNESCO Stone Town seafront, before the House of Wonders
items.description: Every evening the seafront gardens become an open-air feast, grilled seafood, urojo (Zanzibar mix) and the famous 'Zanzibar pizza', the living room of the old town.

items.name: Zanzibar Serena Hotel rooftop bar
credentials: Zanzibar Serena Hotel, restored seafront heritage landmark
items.description: A calm rooftop over the Indian Ocean inside a restored heritage landmark, sundowners with a Taarab soundtrack on Swahili Nights.

items.name: 6 Degrees South Grill & Wine Bar
credentials: Long-standing Shangani seafront bar, grill and wine list
items.description: Three sea-facing terraces on the Shangani waterfront, the reliable spot for a sundowner and a proper glass of wine in the old town.

items.name: Resort beach bars, the north & east coasts
credentials: In-resort beach bars at the credentialed houses (&Beyond Mnemba, Zuri, Kilindi, The Residence)
items.description: The real evening scene sits inside the maison resorts, private beach bars, dhow-deck sundowners and starlit dinners arranged for house guests, away from any crowd.

items.name: Emerson Spice / Emerson on Hurumzi rooftops
credentials: Emerson Zanzibar, celebrated Stone Town rooftop tea houses
items.description: Sunset cocktails on Stone Town's highest rooftops, with the old city's minarets and spires below and live Taarab in the air, the most atmospheric drink on the island.

plan.heading: 4 days in Zanzibar, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive and settle into a suite at Park Hyatt Zanzibar on the seafront.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A quiet walk through Stone Town's lanes with a local historian, the Old Fort, the doors, the spice merchants.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at The Rock's sister table or on the Park Hyatt terrace as the dhows come in.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private tour of a working spice farm inland, then the ruins at Kidichi.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return by early afternoon for the pool and the shallows below the hotel.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Sunset dhow with a chef aboard, seafood grilled as you sail the channel.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Transfer to the north coast and check into a beach villa at &Beyond Mnemba Island or Zuri Zanzibar.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Snorkel the Mnemba atoll with a private boat and guide, over the reef and the turtles.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Barefoot dinner on the sand, the kitchen cooking the day's catch to your table.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A long morning swim, then a spa treatment drawn from the island's own oils.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: A final lunch over the water before the transfer back across the island.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Day room held at the airport hotel, then the evening flight out.

items.name: Stone Town
items.description: The UNESCO old town of carved doors and narrow lanes, atmospheric and historic, best for one or two nights, not the whole trip.

items.name: Matemwe
items.description: Quiet northeast coast opposite Mnemba, with the island's best barefoot-luxury lodges, for couples who want calm and reef access.

items.name: Nungwi
items.description: The lively north tip with deep water that swims at any tide; more energy and more crowds than the east.

events.name: Sauti za Busara
events.note: East Africa's leading music festival fills Stone Town's Old Fort over a long weekend of live African acts.

events.name: Zanzibar International Film Festival (ZIFF)
events.note: Screenings and performances across Stone Town's historic venues, the region's oldest film festival.

events.name: Eid al-Fitr
events.note: On this deeply Muslim island the end of Ramadan brings feasting and celebration; timing shifts each year with the lunar calendar.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Zanzibar is majority-Muslim, so cover shoulders and knees away from the beach, especially in Stone Town; stay on the north-east coast (Matemwe, Michamvi) for calm swimmable water at all tides, and confirm a yellow-fever certificate if arriving from mainland safari.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Abeid Amani Karume International (ZNZ), often via Nairobi or Dar, where a hotel host clears you and a private car (or a short boat for island resorts) carries you to the coast.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver handles the island's roads; along the coast a dhow or speedboat is the elegant way to move between beaches and sandbanks.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Local eSIM/SIM on Airtel or Vodacom is cheap and works across the island; resort Wi-Fi is reliable, connections beyond that patchy.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Tanzanian shilling (TSH), though USD is accepted at resorts; carry small cash for markets and Stone Town, and tip staff and drivers in USD or TSH.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: June-October is the cool dry season with clear skies and calm sea; avoid the long rains of March-May when humidity and downpours peak, and the shorter November rains.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No nonstop from India; cleanest routing is via a Gulf hub (Emirates via Dubai, Qatar via Doha) or Kenya Airways via Nairobi, roughly 12-15 hours in J. Pair it with the Mara on one Kenya Airways itinerary through Nairobi rather than backtracking.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Yellow fever certificate needed if arriving from or transiting Kenya; malaria prophylaxis advised, routine vaccines current. Stone Town calls for modest dress and normal city awareness; the beach resorts are calm. Bottled water only.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Zanzibar's Indian-origin heritage means vegetarian food is easy and Jain is manageable at the better resorts with notice. The Swahili spice cuisine is naturally vegetable-forward; Emerson Spice in Stone Town does a notable rooftop menu.
